settings.headline: Your eye drops are treating the wrong layer
settings.author: The Dewy Team
settings.lead: If your eyes feel gritty by mid-afternoon, sting at the screen, and somehow water for no reason — and every drop you've tried feels great for an hour and then fades — you're not doing anything wrong. You've just been handed the wrong tool for the actual problem. Here's what's really going on, because once you see it you can't un-see it.
settings.intro_body: Most people never get told this part, and it changes how you think about relief.
settings.layers_title: Your tears aren't one thing. They're three.
settings.layers_intro: Most people picture tears as just water. They're not. A healthy tear film has three layers stacked on top of each other, and each one has a job:
settings.layer_oil_desc: Made by tiny glands in your eyelids. Its job is to stop the tears underneath from evaporating. This is the layer that fails most.
settings.layer_water_desc: The big wet middle layer. This is the part most eye drops top up.
settings.layer_mucin_desc: The sticky base that helps everything spread evenly across your eye.
settings.layer_note: Here's the catch: most drops refill the WATER layer. But the layer that's usually failing is the OIL layer on top. That's why the relief washes out in an hour — you're topping up water that has nothing holding it in.
settings.pullquote: When the oil layer thins, your tears evaporate before they can do their job. More water doesn't fix a missing lid on the jar.
settings.agitate_title: Why the oil layer gives out — especially in your 40s and 50s
settings.agitate_body:
Those oil glands along your lash line slow down and clog as we age, and the hormonal shifts of perimenopause speed it up. The oil thickens, the glands block, and less of it reaches your tears. It's gradual, so you adapt — you blink harder, you reach for drops, you assume it's just screens or getting older.

It isn't in your head, and it isn't only age. It's a specific, well-understood mechanism. And the good news about a specific mechanism is that it has a specific first step.
settings.mech_title: What actually helps the oil layer
settings.mech_intro: You can't fix a thickened-oil problem with more water. You warm the oil so it flows again — which is exactly what Dewy is built to do.
settings.mech1_body: Research indicates the eyelid needs to reach around 40°C to soften the thickened oils in the glands. Dewy holds a gentle, even warmth across the whole lid — not a flannel that's scalding then cold in 90 seconds.
settings.mech2_body: Warm compresses fail people because a hot towel is a nuisance, so nobody keeps it up. Dewy is a 10-minute ritual you'll genuinely repeat — and consistency is the whole game here.
settings.mech3_body: Washable and comfortable enough that it becomes the nice part of your evening instead of a chore. That's deliberate — comfort is what turns it into a habit.
settings.mech4_title: Works with your drops, not instead of them
settings.mech4_body: Keep using whatever your optometrist recommends. Dewy addresses the oil layer those drops can't reach — the two do different jobs.
settings.evidence_title: What the eye specialists actually say
settings.evidence_body:
We won't tell you Dewy is a cure, or that it beats anything your optometrist has given you — it isn't and it doesn't, and anyone who says that about a warm mask is being dishonest with you.

What's true: warm-compress and lid-warming therapy is recognised as a first-line approach for evaporative dry eye and meibomian gland dysfunction in the international TFOS DEWS II consensus, and is recommended by major eye-care bodies including the American Optometric Association and American Academy of Ophthalmology. Meibomian gland dysfunction — an oil-layer problem — is the leading cause of dry eye. A warm compress is simply one of the best-evidenced first things you can do at home, often used alongside professional care.

Not a miracle. Just the sensible, specialist-backed first step — done in a way you'll actually stick to.
